Ibn Atiyya includes generosity in paying and collecting debts.","rows":["NASAFI-FULL:v4p90#4/r1","BIQAI-FULL:v6p572/r2","BURSEVI:v8p200#3/r1","BURSEVI:v8p200#3/r6","ALUSI-FULL:v24p123/r3","ELMALILI:41:33-39#2/r3","KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:41:34/r1","IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p16/r4"],"prefer":[],"against":[]},{"position":"Turn away from the offender's harm or refrain from replying.","reasons":"Mujahid recommends turning away; Ali, as quoted by Qurtubi, recommends silence to Qanbar, and Qurtubi adduces poems that silence most frustrates an insulting fool.","rows":["ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p306/r8","QURTUBI-FULL:41:34#2/r6","QURTUBI-FULL:41:34#2/r7","QURTUBI-FULL:41:34#2/r8"],"prefer":[],"against":[]},{"position":"Shake hands affectionately and sincerely when meeting.","reasons":"Ibn al-Arabi applies the verse this way, citing a report that handshaking removes rancor; al-Bara's Prophetic report says two Muslims clasping hands have sins fall away.","rows":["QURTUBI-FULL:41:34/r11","QURTUBI-FULL:41:34#2/r1"],"prefer":[],"against":[]},{"position":"Repel one's own impulses toward vice by practicing virtue.","reasons":"Study Quran explicitly gives this inward application; Biqai includes harm from oneself as well as from others; Qashani contrasts the heart with the lower self and warns that evil for evil grows.","rows":["STUDYQURAN:41:34/r11","BIQAI-FULL:v6p572/r2","QASHANI:41:34-35/r1"],"prefer":[],"against":[]}],"turns_on":"Whether the command is read as a broad practice or a particular form of response; the greeting reports are treated by Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan as a beginning of the broader practice."}
